### Gentrification: Acceleration and Geographic Concentration
Gentrification has intensified significantly since the early 2000s. [Source: ev-1]
The rate of gentrification for eligible lower-income neighborhoods doubled after 2000 compared to the 1990s [Source: ev-1].
Specifically, nearly 20% of neighborhoods with lower incomes and home values experienced gentrification since 2000, whereas only 9% did so during the 1990 decade [Source: ev-2].

### Affordability and Economic Mobility
Housing costs have outpaced income growth, creating affordability crises. [Source: ev-1]
Since 2000, home prices increased by 177%, while median household income grew by only 92% [Source: ev-1].
The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024, representing a 225% increase since January 2000 [Source: ev-1].
In California cities, price-to-income ratios range between 9.6 and 12.2, more than double the national average of 4.7 [Source: ev-1].

### Structural Economic Shifts
The underlying economic structure supporting these changes involves a shift away from manufacturing toward professional services. [Source: ev-1]

Manufacturing jobs fell from 19.5 million in 1979 to under 11.5 million during the pandemic era data points provided, while finance and professional services grew from 12 million to 32 million jobs [Source: ev-1].

This shift concentrated high-income professionals in urban cores, contributing to the "stark divide" where urban centers house both top earners (e.g., Boston’s 80th percentile at $172,476) and low-income service workers (Boston’s 20th percentile at $22,095) [Source: ev-1]
